name: PT Amman Mineral Internasional Tbk

frontmatter.title: Amman Mineral: a copper mine priced for spot, a gold mine still to be built
frontmatter.summary: We initiate on Amman Mineral with a REDUCE. The equity prices copper at the current tight spot print, not at the through-cycle marker our metals desk underwrites, and it pays nothing for the risk that the gold-rich Elang project consumes years of cash before it produces. Our life-of-asset NAV is below the share price on every scenario except a sustained higher copper price, and the balance sheet offers little protection if the cycle turns.
thesis: The market is capitalising copper near spot while our through-cycle marker is materially lower, so the equity carries a mean-reversion risk the price does not reflect.
The 2026 sales shortfall is an inventory-timing effect, not a mine problem, and the volume recovery to the guidance run-rate is already in our base case rather than an upside.
Elang is a genuine gold-rich porphyry, but it needs a multi-year build at a capital intensity the company has not yet disclosed, and our base case charges that spend in full.
The balance sheet has deleveraged quickly, but the interest burden and the absent dividend leave the equity holder with no cash return while the build runs.
Our bull case needs copper above the reviewed through-cycle marker and a cheaper Elang build to exceed today's price at all; the base case, the most likely path, does not.

catalysts.event: Full-year results and the following year's production guidance
Elang final investment decision and owner's cost tender outcome
Concentrator ramp to the expanded nameplate and smelter utilisation

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Amman Mineral Internasional with a REDUCE rating and a target of Rp3,063, against a share price of Rp4,000; that is a total return of -23.4% over the coming year [S2 p.48, S3 p.6]. The call is not a judgement on the quality of the orebody, which is one of the largest copper-gold reserve bases in the world, but on the price paid for it. Our life-of-asset NAV is Rp3,064 per share. The probability-weighted scenario target is Rp3,063, the base case is Rp3,499, and the bull case is Rp4,372, which needs copper above the marker and a cheaper Elang build merely to exceed today's price [S2 p.48, S6].

A caveat on the scenario range is owed to the reader before anything else. The engine's scenario override writes the shocked copper deck into every forecast year, so from FY2031 the shocked price no longer escalates with the deck's long-run path: the bull and the bear both run a flat copper price against costs that keep rising. That is a defect in the scenario tool, not a view about copper, and it distorts the two tails in opposite directions: it suppresses the bull and depresses the bear, so the published Rp3,063 weighted target sits below the value the same model produces once the shock is confined to the explicit years. Run that way, the bear is nearly double the engine figure, the bull is about a quarter higher and stands roughly two-fifths above the current share price, and the weighted target is about a seventh higher, cutting the expected loss roughly in half. The base case, which carries half the weight and sets our rating, uses no override and is untouched. We publish the engine target as the official number because a script fix is outside our remit and is flagged to OPS, but the honest read is that the expected return is roughly half the headline figure, and that the distribution is far closer to symmetric than the published range suggests [S2 p.101, S6].

The single most important number in this report is the copper price. The metals desk's reviewed through-cycle marker is US$11,000/t, while the metal currently prints at US$13,708/t [S2 p.101, S3 p.6]. A miner with a long reserve life is a claim on the whole price path, not on today's print, and at the through-cycle marker the equity is worth less than the market pays. We are therefore underwriting a normalisation of copper rather than a collapse: our bear case carries copper below the marker rather than at a distressed level, and even our bear case leaves the Elang reserves in place rather than writing them off [S6].

The second driver is volume, and here the market may be misreading the last two quarters. Copper sold fell to 107.5 in the last full year because concentrate was stockpiled ahead of the smelter and refined metal was still being built in inventory during the current year, not because the mine was exhausted [S2 p.107, S3 p.21]. We model a recovery to the guidance run-rate of 220 in the coming year and then a plateau at the expanded plant's physical capacity, which is the most likely path rather than the cautious one [S2 p.107, S5].

The third driver is Elang. Its reserve statement is exceptional: the deposit contains 8,242 of contained copper and a large gold credit, and the ore is far richer in gold per unit of copper than Batu Hijau [S6]. That is why we step the realisation ratio up when Elang enters the mine plan. It is also why the project is expensive, and we charge the build in full through the middle of the forecast rather than treating it as free optionality [S3 p.5, S6].

The result is a distribution whose central case does not reach the share price. The base case is Rp3,499 on the reviewed marker, the bull case is Rp4,372 and the bear case is Rp882, where a lower copper price meets a twenty per cent Elang capex overrun and operating leverage runs the wrong way. The equity is not expensive because the asset is poor; it is expensive because the price already assumes an outcome better than our most likely one [S2 p.48, S6].

Amman Mineral Internasional is an Indonesian copper-gold company that owns the Batu Hijau mine and is developing the Elang deposit, both in West Sumbawa Regency, West Nusa Tenggara [S2 p.48]. The company holds almost all of its operating subsidiary, PT Amman Mineral Nusa Tenggara, which holds the mining licence and runs the integrated chain from pit to cathode and refined gold [S2 p.48]. Batu Hijau has produced cumulatively more than ten billion pounds of copper and about eleven million ounces of gold since commercial production began, which places it among the most significant copper-gold mines in the country [S2 p.48].

The business has changed shape in the last two years. AMMN has moved from selling copper and gold in concentrate to operating a smelter and a precious-metals refinery, so it now sells copper cathode, refined gold, refined silver and sulphuric acid as well as concentrate [S2 p.52, S4 p.5]. The smelter has a design capacity of 220 of copper cathode and the refinery is designed to produce 579 of refined gold a year, alongside silver and selenium [S2 p.52]. That integration is the strategic centre of the story: it captures the downstream margin, satisfies Indonesia's domestic-processing requirement, and converts a concentrate exporter into a refiner with a domestic franchise [S2 p.52, S3 p.5].

The products and their weight in revenue are best read from the physical volumes rather than from a segment note, because the company reports one integrated copper-gold segment [S2 p.226]. In the last full year it sold 107.5 of copper and 170 of gold, and the presentation shows cathode production of 79.8 and refined gold production of 124.7 as the new downstream streams ramped [S4 p.5]. Copper is the volume anchor and gold is the margin swing: the gold credit is a large share of revenue per tonne of copper, which is why the realised-price ratio in our model is well above one [S2 p.98].

The growth plan has two legs. The first is the processing plant, which has been expanded from a concentrator of roughly the mid-thirty-million-tonne class to a nameplate of 85 million tonnes a year, with first ore through the expanded circuit in the middle of the current year [S5, S2 p.53]. The second is Elang, where the definitive feasibility study was completed and the owner's cost tender is in progress, with a final investment decision targeted for the following year and first ore projected after Batu Hijau's mine life ends [S3 p.5, S6]. The two legs are linked: the expanded plant is sized to take Elang ore, so the capital spent on the concentrator is only fully utilised once Elang is built [S2 p.53, S5].

The reserve base is the reason the company matters. Batu Hijau's reserve is 777 million tonnes of ore, and Elang's reserve is 8,242 of contained copper within a much larger tonnage, with a gold credit that the reserve statement puts at a level that changes the revenue mix when it enters the plan [S6]. The company describes Elang as a super-giant copper-gold porphyry, a classification that speaks to scale rather than to grade, and the grade is the key modelling variable because it sets both the copper output at the expanded plant and the gold credit per tonne [S2 p.48, S6].

Ownership is concentrated. The register shows PT Sumber Gemilang Persada at just under a third, Medco Energi at about a fifth, PT AP Investment at about a sixth, PT Pesona Sukses Cemerlang and SAJIR LLC at smaller blocks, and the public at under a fifth [S2 p.48]. The free float is 22.8% of the shares, which is enough for index inclusion and daily liquidity but not enough to make the register dispersed [S2 p.48]. We do not apply the konglo lens to this name: the controlling shareholders are a diversified resources and energy group rather than a single-family conglomerate, and the governance analysis in section six is on the register as disclosed rather than on a group-structure overlay [S2 p.48].

The licence and fiscal terms are Indonesian. The company operates under a special mining business licence for production operations, converted from the original contract of work, and it pays government royalties on copper and gold [S2 p.48, S2 p.101]. The royalty schedule was raised in April of the last year, with copper cathode moving to a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit rate and gold to a high-teens rate, which is the single largest change in the unit economics since the smelter started [S2 p.101]. Export permits for concentrate were granted in the same period, so the policy risk is the timing of permits rather than an outright ban [S2 p.101, S4 p.5].

The company employed 2,216 people at the last disclosure, which is small relative to the tonnage moved and reflects the contractor-heavy operating model typical of large Indonesian open pits [S2 p.48]. The operating footprint is a single district, so the asset base is geographically concentrated: Batu Hijau and Elang are in the same regency, which lowers logistics cost but concentrates community, water and seismic risk in one place [S2 p.48, S2 p.53].

Copper is the metal that sets the company's revenue, and the market is currently tight. The reviewed deck carries a through-cycle marker of US$11,000/t against a spot print of US$13,708/t, a gap of roughly a quarter that the desk treats as cyclical tightness rather than a new equilibrium [S2 p.101, S3 p.6]. The tightness is visible in the realised prices: the company sold cathode at a price well above the marker in the current year, and its concentrate realisation was also strong [S3 p.7]. The question for a long-life miner is not whether copper is tight today but whether the marginal cost of supply has moved up permanently, and the deck's answer is that it has not moved by as much as spot implies [S2 p.101].

Gold is the second price in the revenue mix. The reviewed marker is US$4,300/oz against a spot print of US$4,075/oz, so gold is close to its through-cycle level rather than at a spike [S2 p.101]. Silver is the third, at a marker of US$65.0/oz, and it is a small credit [S2 p.101]. The practical implication is that the revenue risk in our model is concentrated in copper: a gold move of the same percentage changes value by less, because the gold credit is smaller than the copper base even after the Elang step-up [S6].

The company's own reserve statement is struck at a lower copper price than the desk carries: copper 4.00 a pound and gold 2,500 an ounce [S6]. That is the conservative price at which the reserves are booked for reporting, not a forecast of the market, and it sits roughly a fifth below the reviewed marker; we value on the reviewed series because a reserve price is chosen to make the orebody robust, while the plan price is the right anchor for the downside and is where our bear case effectively lands [S6].

Copper porphyry deposits are large, low-grade bodies of disseminated sulphide minerals. The economic
question is not whether the metal is there but how much ore must be moved and milled for each unit of
contained metal, which is why throughput, grade and recovery dominate the cost curve. A concentrator
turns the ore into a concentrate that must be smelted and refined before it becomes saleable cathode;
the smelter is therefore a fixed-cost toll gate that rewards scale and utilisation. Gold and silver
report partly to the concentrate and partly to refinery products, so a copper mine with a gold credit
behaves like a copper producer with a call option on the gold price. Indonesian policy has pushed
miners to build domestic smelting capacity rather than export raw concentrate, which raises the
capital intensity of the sector but captures more of the value chain inside the country.

The competitive landscape is global at the top and concentrated at home. AMMN is a domestic scale producer with a reserve base that the company describes as one of the largest copper-equivalent bases globally [S2 p.48]. The listed domestic peer set is thin, which is why the engine cannot form a peer-median EV/EBITDA benchmark and why we lean on a life-of-asset NAV rather than a relative multiple [S2 p.48]. Competition for capital is with global porphyry projects, not with the domestic gold names, and the relevant comparison is cost-curve position rather than market share [S2 p.91].

The cost position is the moat. The company reports an adjusted unit cash cost that is negative after by-product credits in the last full year, and the current-year figure is also negative [S2 p.91, S3 p.11]. A negative unit cost means the gold, silver and acid credits cover the cash cost of the copper, so the mine can survive a copper price well below the through-cycle marker without closing. That is a first-quartile position by construction, and it is the strongest argument against a bear case that assumes distress [S2 p.91]. The cost advantage is not permanent: it depends on gold credits, diesel and power costs, and the strip ratio, all of which can move [S2 p.100].

The five-forces picture is favourable on rivalry and substitution and weaker on buyer power and regulation. Rivalry is global and disciplined by the cost curve, and copper has no close substitute at scale in electrical applications, which supports the through-cycle price [S2 p.101]. Buyer power sits with global traders and smelters, but the integrated smelter reduces the company's exposure to treatment and refining charges [S2 p.52]. Supplier power is real in diesel, power and consumables, which is why the model carries a fuel sensitivity, and regulation is the binding constraint: royalties, export permits and the domestic-processing obligation are set by policy rather than by the company [S2 p.101, S2 p.52].

The macro frame the desk carries is cautious. The house view is a balance-of-payments pressure regime with a cautious tilt, neutral on the commodity complex as a single beta, and it does not favour or penalise this name on the macro tilt alone [S2 p.101]. The rupiah assumption is Rp18,350/USD to the dollar, which matters because the company earns in dollars and is valued in rupiah [S2 p.101]. A weaker rupiah raises the rupiah target mechanically without changing the dollar value of the business, and we treat that as a translation effect rather than a thesis [S2 p.101].

The last full year was a transition year, and the reported numbers need to be read with that in mind. Revenue was US$1,847, EBITDA on the company's presentation basis was US$1,057, and net profit was US$258, well below the prior year because copper and gold sales volumes fell during the smelter ramp and interest costs rose [S2 p.98, S4 p.5]. The presentation EBITDA is higher than the income-statement build of US$921 because the presentation adds back items that the statutory accounts do not isolate, and we use the lower figure in the model so that the forecast is not flattered [S2 p.100, S4 p.5].

The cost structure is the key to the model. Cost of revenue was US$1,011, of which government royalties were US$219 and depreciation and amortisation was US$247, leaving cash cost of about 5,065 per tonne of copper sold [S2 p.100, S2 p.101]. That derivation matters: it is the only way to reconcile the reported EBITDA with a per-tonne cash cost that can be forecast. The engine's calibration now re-prices the current year at last year's copper and volume but with this year's by-product credit, so it shows a positive gap that is the gold mix, not a cost error; the cash cost and the royalty rate are the ones the last actual implies [S2 p.100, F5, F17]. The cash cost is gross of the gold and silver credits, which sit in the realisation ratio, so the two lines together reproduce the margin [S2 p.98].

The balance sheet has improved sharply during the current year. Net debt had fallen from its peak at the last reported date as free cash flow was applied to repayment, and the company reports net debt to EBITDA of about two times [S3 p.6]. Debt was repaid with sales cash in the nine months, and the interest burden is still the largest call on earnings before tax [S3 p.6, S2 p.102]. The average cost of debt in the accounts is in the high single digits, which is why the interest line is large relative to EBIT in a down year [S2 p.102].

Working capital is the line that distorts the cash flow. In the last full year operating working capital was almost nine-tenths of revenue because concentrate was stockpiled ahead of the smelter and refined metal was being built in inventory [S8 p.76]. That is a one-off build, not a permanent feature of the business, and we normalise the ratio to the pre-commissioning level for the forecast [S8 p.76, S2 p.98]. The normalisation releases working capital in the first forecast year, which is why free cash flow is strong even before the volume recovery is complete [S8 p.76].

Our forecast path is physical rather than price-led. We model copper sold of 180 in the current year, recovering to 220 at the guidance run-rate, then declining as Phase Eight grades normalise and the stockpile is worked down, before Elang enters the plan and lifts the plateau to 250 [S2 p.107, S3 p.7, S6]. The current-year number is below the production guidance because sales, not mine output, are the constraint: the company produced more concentrate than it sold while the smelter was commissioning [S3 p.7, S3 p.21].

The current year is calibrated to what has already been reported, not to the last audited year alone. Nine-month net sales were US$3,238, EBITDA US$1,833 and net income US$880 [S3 p.6], so the full-year forecast must sit above those actuals rather than imply a fourth-quarter collapse: our US$4,436 of revenue and US$1,199 of net income attributable to shareholders leave a fourth quarter broadly in line with the third, on 180 of copper sold for the year [S3 p.6, p.7].

The resulting financial path has three phases. The first is the recovery: revenue rises to US$4,436 as volume and prices normalise, and EBITDA rises to US$2,552 [S3 p.5, S6]. The second is the Elang build: capital expenditure steps up to 6,000 per tonne of copper sold, free cash flow turns negative in the trough years, and net debt rises again before the project delivers [S3 p.5, S6]. The third is the plateau: once Elang is running, revenue reaches US$5,599 and the gold credit lifts EBITDA to US$3,294 in that same year, on a margin of 58.8% [S6, F7].

The capex estimate is the largest judgement in the forecast. The company has not published an Elang capital budget, so we use its own recent capital intensity as the proxy: it spent US$1,373 in the last full year and US$1,792 the year before on Phase Eight, the smelter, the concentrator and the power plant [S2 p.104]. Spreading a similar annual intensity over the build years is the most defensible estimate available, and we flag it as an estimate rather than a disclosure [S2 p.104, S6]. If the project comes in cheaper, the target rises; if it overruns, the target falls by more, because the spend sits before the cash flows [S6].

Capital allocation is conservative by necessity. The company has said it does not expect to pay dividends until its major capital programmes are complete, so the base case carries no dividend through the forecast [S2 p.107]. It announced a small buy-back in the current year, which we treat as cash leaving the company rather than as a permanent reduction in the share count because the execution is not disclosed [S3 p.5, F22]. The equity holder is therefore paid in asset growth rather than cash, and the return depends entirely on the market's view of the assets [S2 p.107].

Earnings quality carries three flags. The first is the gap between reported EBITDA and the income-statement build, which we resolve conservatively [S4 p.5, S2 p.100]. The second is the negative operating cash flow in the last full year, caused by the working-capital build and the smelter commissioning, which should reverse as inventory unwinds [S8 p.76, S2 p.98]. The third is the depreciation charge, which is low relative to the capital spent, so the statutory earnings may be flattered by a depreciation lag even as cash flow is depressed; our model uses the disclosed depreciation per tonne rather than extrapolating the capex [S2 p.100, F15]. None of these changes the cash economics, but they explain why the reported profit and the cash flow tell different stories [S2 p.100].

We value AMMN on a life-of-asset discounted cash flow, which is the method the commodity-producer card requires for a depleting asset [S6]. The primary method carries the great majority of the weight, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check at through-cycle earnings; we exclude P/BV because a mine's book value is a depreciating historical cost rather than a measure of the orebody [S2 p.104]. The engine cannot form a peer-median EV/EBITDA benchmark from the listed domestic set, so the cross-check is shown for context rather than used to set the target [S2 p.48].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro inputs. The risk-free rate is 4.86%, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.23%, and the Indonesia country risk premium is 2.46%; with an unlevered beta of 1.00 and gearing of 36.5%, the levered beta is 1.28, the cost of equity is 14.2%, and the weighted average cost of capital is 11.8% [S2 p.101]. The pre-tax cost of debt in the build is 6.9%, the house marginal rate, below the high-single-digit coupon the accounts actually pay; rather than discount at a rate kinder than the company's own debt, we add a company premium of under a percentage point to the cost of equity so the WACC lands at the level implied by the high-single-digit rate the assumptions carry on its facilities [S0, S2 p.102].

The orebody that carries the long-dated value is in the audited reserve statement, not only in the press: the annual report's JORC table shows Elang's 17.8 billion pounds of contained copper and its gold at a grade that gives about three and a quarter ounces of gold per tonne of contained copper [S2 p.88, p.93], which is the ratio the realisation step-up in section three uses. The cash flow runs thirty years, about two-thirds of the reserve life at the current volume, rather than to a terminal value; the reserve base would carry the DCF some four decades out and we do not capitalise a nominal copper escalation that far, so the omitted tail is a known conservatism and not a terminal value in disguise [S6, F7]. We model the expanded plant at its physical capacity, the Elang reserve at its disclosed grade, and the gold credit at the reserve ratio, with no terminal growth because the asset depletes [S6, F7]. The omitted tail is small at our discount rate: the years beyond the window would add value, but discounted at the cost of capital we use their present value is a low single-digit percentage of the enterprise value, so we treat the truncation as a stated conservatism rather than a hidden valuation input [S2 p.101, F7]. The result is an enterprise value of US$17,135, from which we deduct the latest balance-sheet net debt, minorities and the post-balance-sheet buy-back, and add the disclosed investments, to reach an equity value of Rp3,064 per share [S2 p.48, S3 p.6]. The base-case target of Rp3,499 rolls that value forward at the cost of equity for the twelve-month horizon [S2 p.101].

One caveat belongs in front of the scenario weighting. The engine's scenario override writes the shocked copper deck into every forecast year, so after the deck's explicit horizon the shocked price stops escalating and the bull and the bear both carry a flat metal price against rising costs. The defect suppresses the bull and depresses the bear; it does not touch the base case, which is the whole of the method weight and the origin of our rating. Section five sets out the corrected range, and the published weighted target remains the engine output, flagged to OPS [S2 p.101, S6].

The gap to the share price is the whole call. The market pays Rp4,000 for an asset we value at Rp3,064 on the through-cycle marker, a premium of roughly a third [S2 p.48, S6]. That premium is not explained by the balance sheet, which is deleveraging, or by the volume path, which we already take to the guidance run-rate. It is explained by the copper price: the share price is consistent with copper near the current spot print rather than at the through-cycle marker, which is the definition of a procyclical valuation [S2 p.101].

The cross-checks tell the same story from a different angle. On our forecast, the shares trade on an EV/EBITDA of 8.0 times for the current year and 8.2 times for the next, which looks undemanding until one remembers that those earnings are struck at prices above the through-cycle marker [S2 p.101]. The P/BV is 2.4 times, which is not a meaningful anchor for a depleting asset [S2 p.104]. The multiple cross-check is therefore not a support for the price; it is a restatement of the same price assumption [S2 p.101].

Sensitivity is dominated by copper, then by the Elang capital estimate, then by the discount rate. A fifteen per cent move in copper is worth more than a percentage point of WACC, and the Elang build is the largest single swing after price because the spend sits before the cash flows [S6]. One caveat on the grid: it is keyed to the gold deck, not to copper, because the model carries the gold credit inside the realisation ratio rather than as a separate revenue line, and every FX column is identical because the company reports and borrows in dollars and the rupiah only translates the result [S2 p.102, S3 p.7]. The grid therefore understates the copper sensitivity that the scenarios in section five actually shock; the bear and bull cases apply their shocks to the full model rather than to a single line [S2 p.101].

The reverse-DCF check does not produce a value because the share price sits outside the range the solver can bracket: the solver is keyed to the gold deck, the credit that sits inside our realisation ratio, and no gold multiplier between one fifth and five times the marker brings our value to the share price, because it is the copper path that sets it [S2 p.101, S3 p.7]. That is itself the answer. The market is not pricing the through-cycle marker; it is pricing something closer to spot, and the solver's failure is the arithmetic expression of that gap rather than a statement about gold [S2 p.101].

It is worth being explicit about what would change our mind. If the copper deficit proves structural and the through-cycle marker moves up toward the spot print, the base case rises toward the bull case, and the equity becomes fairly valued rather than expensive [S2 p.101]. If Elang's capital budget comes in below our proxy, the middle years of the forecast improve and the target rises [S6]. If the rupiah weakens materially, the rupiah target rises mechanically even with an unchanged dollar value [S2 p.101]. None of these is in the base case, and each is a reason the rating is a negative view on price rather than on the asset [S6].

The first risk is copper. The share price is sensitive to a metal that is currently above its through-cycle marker, and a normalisation of the kind the deck assumes would take the equity well below our base case [S2 p.101]. The bear case applies a fifteen per cent discount to the marker, a five per cent volume cut and a twenty per cent Elang capex overrun, and it produces a target of Rp882: at that copper price the marker has fallen close to the 4.00 a pound the company itself uses for its reserves, and the capital programme is fixed while the revenue is not [S6]. The bear is the case where the Elang budget, the largest undisclosed number in the forecast, lands high at the same time as the cycle turns [S3 p.5, S6].

The second risk is Elang execution. The project is not yet at final investment decision, the owner's cost tender is still running, and the capital budget is undisclosed; our estimate is built from the company's own recent intensity rather than from a project estimate [S3 p.5, S6]. A cost overrun or a delay pushes the cash flows to the right and raises the net debt carried through the build, which is the mechanism that makes the bear case so weak [S6]. The project is also the reason the bull case is not much stronger than the base: the upside is real but it is back-ended [S6]. We do not add a project-financing case to the bull: the model is an enterprise DCF whose discount rate already carries the group's gearing, so how the Elang build is funded changes the split between debt and equity holders and the interest tax shield already in the WACC, not the enterprise value that the target is struck on [S2 p.102].

The third risk is policy. Royalties were raised in the last year, export permits are granted periodically, and the domestic-processing obligation shapes the capital programme [S2 p.101, S2 p.52]. A further royalty increase or a change in the permit regime would hit the realised margin directly, and the government's fiscal take is already a material line in the cost build [S2 p.101]. We do not model a policy shock in the base case because the current terms are disclosed, but it is a live risk in a name where the state is both regulator and royalty holder [S2 p.101].

The fourth risk is the smelter. The ramp has had operational incidents, including repair-related downtime at the flash converting furnace and the acid plant, and the current-year utilisation is the test of whether the integrated model works [S2 p.52]. If the smelter runs below design capacity, the company sells more concentrate and less cathode, which changes the realised price and the cost base [S2 p.52, S3 p.7]. The current-year results show the smelter performing at design capacity, which is encouraging, but the track record is short [S3 p.5].

The fifth risk is the balance sheet. Net debt is still material relative to a trough EBITDA, and the interest cost is high enough to absorb a large share of EBIT in a weak year [S2 p.102]. The company has deleveraged quickly, which reduces the risk, but the Elang build will consume cash at the same time as the copper price may be normalising, so the cushion is thinner than the current ratio suggests [S3 p.6, S6]. A refinancing at a higher rate would hit the equity directly [S2 p.102].

The sixth risk is geological and operational. Phase Eight grades, recovery rates and the strip ratio are the variables that determine the volume path, and the reserve statement is a statement about the orebody rather than about the mine plan [S2 p.107, S6]. A grade reconciliation shortfall would reduce volume and raise unit cost at the same time, which is the operating leverage that the bear case captures [S6]. The company has a long operating history at Batu Hijau, which mitigates but does not remove the risk [S2 p.48].

The seventh risk is governance and liquidity. The register is concentrated, the free float is 22.8%, and the controlling shareholders can influence strategy and capital allocation [S2 p.48]. We do not apply the konglo lens, but a concentrated register is a governance consideration in its own right, and the absence of a dividend means the minority holder depends on the controller's capital allocation [S2 p.107]. Liquidity is adequate but not deep, and a large shareholder transaction would move the price [S2 p.48].

The scenario table sets out the three cases. The base case is the through-cycle marker with the volume recovery and the Elang build, and it produces Rp3,499. The bear case is a lower copper price with a smaller volume base and the same capital programme, and it produces Rp882. The bull case is a higher copper price with a stronger volume outcome, and it produces Rp4,372. The probabilities are symmetric around the base case.

The last point on the scenario table is a flaw, and we state it plainly rather than leave it in the number. The engine's override writes the shocked copper deck into every forecast year, so from FY2031 the bull and the bear both hold a flat metal price while the mine's costs keep escalating; the deck's own long-run path, by contrast, rises by roughly the dollar inflation rate each year. The freeze is therefore not a view but a mechanical artifact, and it cuts both ways: the bull is understated because it never earns the escalation the base case gets, and the bear is understated in its deficit because its flat revenue is set against rising costs. Re-running the same shocks confined to the deck's explicit years and its long-run value, which is the arithmetic the tool should perform, gives a bear that nearly doubles, a bull about a quarter higher and roughly two-fifths above the current share price, and a weighted target about a seventh higher than the published one, so the expected loss roughly halves and the distribution becomes close to symmetric around the base. The drivers behind those cases are unchanged and sourced: copper at fifteen per cent either side of the reviewed US$11,000/t marker [S2 p.101], volume five per cent either side of the sales path [F1, F11], and Elang capital twenty per cent either side of the company's own recent intensity, because the budget is undisclosed and the owner's cost tender is still running [S3 p.5, S6]. The base case, which carries half the weight and sets the rating, is the only one of the three that the defect leaves alone, and it is below the share price: the rating rests there, not on a tail we know is mismeasured [S2 p.101, S6].

The signposts that would change the view are specific. A sustained copper price above the through-cycle marker would move us toward the bull case; a break below it would move us toward the bear case [S2 p.101]. The Elang final investment decision and the owner's cost tender outcome are the next company-specific catalysts [S3 p.5, S6]. The quarterly cathode output and the unit cash cost are the operating tests, and the net debt trajectory through the build is the balance-sheet test [S3 p.6, S3 p.11]. We would revisit the rating on any of these before the next scheduled refresh [S6].

The shareholder register is the starting point. PT Sumber Gemilang Persada holds just over thirty per cent, Medco Energi holds about a fifth, PT AP Investment holds about a sixth, and the remaining blocks are split between PT Pesona Sukses Cemerlang, SAJIR LLC and the public [S2 p.48]. The free float is 22.8%, and the company holds a small treasury position from the buy-back [S2 p.48, S3 p.5]. A stable, concentrated register is a positive for governance continuity but a negative for minority influence [S2 p.48].

Related-party dealings are disclosed at the subsidiary level. The operating subsidiary is almost wholly owned, with a tiny residual held by PT AP Investment, which is itself a shareholder of the parent [S2 p.48]. That structure is common in Indonesian resource groups and is not by itself a red flag, but it means the minority holder should watch for transactions between the group and its affiliates [S2 p.48]. We found no disclosed related-party transaction that changes the earnings picture in the last year [S2 p.48].

The board and audit arrangements are conventional for an IDX large cap. The company reports an independent commissioner structure and an audit committee, and the annual report carries the usual governance disclosures [S2]. The auditor's opinion is unqualified in the last set of accounts [S2]. We did not find a restatement, a qualification or a material weakness disclosure in the record, which is a clean governance signal [S2].

The earnings-quality contract is stated rather than implied. On the accrual side, net profit exceeded free cash flow in each of the last two years: US$637 of attributable profit against US$-773 of free cash flow, and US$249 against US$-1,297, with a working-capital build of US$720 in the last year on top of US$132 the year before [S2 p.98, S8 p.76]. The accrual gap is therefore large and positive, and it is a timing and classification effect rather than a manipulation: the working capital is concentrate and refined metal awaiting sale, and the interest line, not a capitalised cost, absorbs the difference between EBITDA of US$921 and attributable profit [S2 p.100, S2 p.102]. Cash conversion, measured as free cash flow over EBITDA, is negative in the last year and improves as the inventory unwinds in the current year, when free cash flow turns to US$2,000 [S8 p.76]. We classify the accrual flag as optics, the working-capital flag as a disclosed cycle effect, and the depreciation-timing flag as a conservatism we correct rather than carry [S2 p.100, F5].

On the market side, we checked the listing status and found no special notation, unusual market activity notice, suspension or delisting warning in the archived record, and no board transfer disclosed in the annual report [S2]. The related-party share of revenue is not disclosed as a revenue line and we found no material related-party sales; what is disclosed are balances — long-term related- party assets and trade payables of a few million dollars against a balance sheet more than three orders of magnitude larger — so the related-party percentage of revenue is, on the evidence, not material [S2 p.14, S2 p.15]. Each of the three earnings-quality flags is thus classified and attributed: none changes the cash economics, and none is a manipulation signal [S2 p.98, S8 p.76].

Capital returns are deliberately deferred. The company has said it does not expect to pay dividends until its major capital programmes are complete, so the minority holder is not paid while the build runs [S2 p.107]. The buy-back announced in the current year is small relative to the market capitalisation and is treated as a return of cash rather than as a signal about the share price [S3 p.5, F22]. The dividend record is therefore not a support for the valuation, and the market's anchor is NAV rather than yield [S2 p.107].

Indonesian mining licences are granted for defined terms and can be extended, but the state retains
control over royalties, export permissions and domestic-processing obligations. A company that builds
a smelter satisfies the processing requirement and captures the refining margin, but it also takes on
fixed costs and operating complexity that a pure miner avoids. Community relations, water management
and tailings stewardship are the environmental issues that matter most for a large open pit, and they
are managed through permits and periodic audits rather than through market mechanisms. Governance in
concentrated registers turns on related-party dealings and capital allocation, because the minority
holder has limited ability to change either.

The environmental and social exposure is typical of a large copper-gold open pit: land disturbance, tailings and water management, dust and emissions from the smelter, and community development in a single regency [S2 p.53]. The company reports rehabilitation of several hundred hectares and a lower-emission energy transition through LNG and a combined-cycle power plant, which are the right directions but are early in delivery [S2 p.53]. The smelter's acid plant is both an environmental control and a revenue stream, so the environmental and commercial incentives are aligned [S2 p.52].

Safety is the social issue with the highest tail risk. The company reports a safety-first operating culture and a programme of incident reduction, but a large open pit with contractors and heavy equipment carries inherent risk [S2 p.53]. A serious incident would affect the licence to operate and the production path at the same time, which is a risk that does not appear in the cash flow model [S2 p.53]. We treat it as a qualitative governance and ESG discount rather than as a modelled scenario [S2 p.53].

The governance conclusion is neutral to slightly negative. The register is concentrated, the controlling shareholders are sophisticated, and the disclosure is adequate but not exceptional [S2 p.48]. The absence of a dividend while the build runs is rational for the company but removes a governance discipline that cash returns provide [S2 p.107]. We do not apply the konglo lens, and we do not find a governance fact that justifies a separate valuation overlay [S2 p.48].

The calendar is dominated by the Elang decision. The owner's cost tender is in progress, the final investment decision is targeted for the following year, and first ore is projected after Batu Hijau's mine life ends [S3 p.5, S6]. The outcome of the tender is the single most important company-specific event for the valuation because it sets the capital number that our estimate currently proxies [S6]. A lower cost outcome would lift the middle years of the forecast; a higher one would deepen the bear case [S6].

The operating catalysts are quarterly. The smelter and refinery are running at design capacity, and the market will watch whether that persists through the next set of results [S3 p.5]. The expanded concentrator is in commissioning, and the ramp to nameplate is the test of the volume path [S5]. The unit cash cost is the cleanest read on the cost base, and the company reports it quarterly [S3 p.11]. We would update the volume path if the cathode output or the concentrate sales diverge from the guidance run-rate [S3 p.7].

The financial catalysts are the full-year results and the debt trajectory. Net debt fell during the current year as free cash flow was applied to repayment, and the question is whether that continues into the Elang build or reverses [S3 p.6]. The buy-back execution is a minor catalyst but a signal about management's view of the share price [S3 p.5, F22]. A dividend announcement is unlikely while the capital programme runs, and we do not model one [S2 p.107].

The policy catalysts are the royalty and permit regime. The royalty schedule was raised in the last year, and any further change would hit the realised margin [S2 p.101]. Export permits are granted periodically, and a delay would shift sales between concentrate and cathode [S2 p.101, S3 p.7]. The government's downstreaming policy is the strategic backdrop, and it is supportive of the integrated model as long as the smelter runs [S2 p.52].

The market catalysts are the copper and gold prices. The share price is more sensitive to copper than to gold, and the through-cycle marker is the reference point for our rating [S2 p.101]. A sustained move in copper toward the spot print would change the valuation; a move back toward the marker would validate the REDUCE [S2 p.101]. Gold matters through the by-product credit, and the Elang step-up makes the gold price more important after the project enters the plan [S6].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are copper sold, cathode output, unit cash cost, the strip ratio and grade, capital expenditure, net debt and the Elang tender outcome [S3 p.7, S3 p.11, S6]. The first three tell us whether the operating recovery is real; the next two tell us whether the balance sheet can carry the build; the last tells us whether the valuation's largest estimate is converging [S6]. We will refresh the model when the full-year results or the Elang decision lands, whichever comes first [S3 p.5].

bear.narrative: The copper cycle rolls over before the through-cycle marker: the deck's FY2026E 13,692/t is a spot spike and the bear carries the copper price 15% below the 11,000/t deck path as Chinese property demand stays weak and Indonesian supply arrives, while smelter throughput and Phase 8 grade reconciliation shave 5% off copper sold. The Elang build overruns the base capital intensity by 20% as the owner's cost tender lands high, so operating leverage runs the wrong way and the balance sheet carries more debt through the build. At 0.85x the deck path, copper in FY2027E is about US$9,350/t, within 6% of the US$8,818/t (US$4.00/lb) price at which the company itself books the Elang reserve [S6]; the bear does not go below it. The royalty is carried at the LK's 11.9% effective rate [S2 p.101, F17]; no extra haircut is stacked, and the bear does not zero Elang: its reserves and first-ore date are disclosed [S6].

bull.narrative: The copper deficit persists: the deck's 11,000/t through-cycle marker proves too low against electrification demand and Indonesian supply discipline, so the bull carries copper 15% above it. The 85 Mtpa plant runs at nameplate and Phase 8 grade reconciliation beats plan, adding 5% to copper sold, and Elang's FID lands in 2027 with first ore on schedule and the owner's cost tender 20% below the base intensity. Gold stays at the deck's 4,300/oz. The upside is capped by the same 11.9% effective royalty [S2 p.101, F17]; the mirror of the bear's capex overrun is a capex underspend, not project financing, because the DCF is an enterprise valuation whose WACC already carries the modelled gearing [S2 p.102].

assumptions.label: Copper sales volume plan (kt Cu, all products)
assumptions.basis: The model is on copper metal sold, matching the LK's own sales metric. FY2026E 180 kt: 9M2026 copper sales were 98.3 kt of cathode plus 73 Mlbs (33.1 kt) of copper in concentrate = 131.4 kt, and Q3/Q4 sell refined metal only at about the Q3 cathode run-rate (50 kt in Q3), so the fourth quarter adds roughly 49 kt on the latest actual, not the 220 kt full-year production guidance [S3 p.7, p.14, p.21; S2 p.107, F11]. Inventory, not mine output, is the timing difference: 2025 ended with concentrate stockpiled ahead of the smelter and 9M2026 still built refined-metal inventory [S8 p.76, S3 p.21]. FY2027E 220 kt is the 2026 guidance run-rate at design smelter utilisation (220,000 t contained copper, F11); FY2028E-FY2030E 215/205/195 kt hold that level as Phase 8 grades normalise. FY2031E 170 kt is the last full Batu Hijau year (mine life to 2031/2032, F23). FY2032E 220 kt introduces Elang first ore through the expanded 85 Mtpa concentrator [S5, F25]; the ceiling is physical, not a demand view: 85 Mt at the 0.319% Cu reserve grade [S6, F7] is 271 kt of contained copper, about 239 kt at 88% recovery, and blending higher-grade Batu Hijau stockpile ore lifts the plateau to 250 kt. FY2033E-FY2035E 240/248/250 kt are therefore the Elang ramp to the plant's maximum, not a 320 kt extrapolation that the concentrator cannot deliver at reserve grade. The plateau is held to the end of the explicit window; no volume decline is assumed before the sourced mine-life end.

assumptions.label: Realised copper price plus gold/silver credits / copper benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual, not on a forecast spike: FY2025 net sales of US$1,846.5m [S0, S2 p.98] over 107.50 kt of copper sold [F1] at the deck's FY2025A copper average of US$10,636.91/t gives 1.615x. The premium over the copper benchmark is the by-product credit: FY2025 gold sales of 169.55 koz [F3] at US$3,466.09/oz are 0.514x of copper revenue per tonne at the deck ratio, with the remaining ~0.10x silver, sulphuric acid and concentrate/cathode realisation differences [S2 p.98, S4 p.5]. FY2025's 1.615x is the calibration anchor, not the FY2026E ratio: 2025 sales were depressed by an inventory build (169.55 koz of gold sold against 227.5 koz produced once the refined-gold stream is counted [F3, F10, F20]), so the last-actual ratio understates the steady-state by-product credit. The 9M2026 actual sets FY2026E: net sales of US$3,238m over 131.4 kt of copper sold is US$24,642/t, 1.80x the FY2026E deck copper of US$13,692/t, on 294 koz of gold sold (2.24 oz per tonne, about 0.78x of copper revenue) [S3 p.6, p.7, p.9]. 1.80x is therefore used for FY2026E-FY2031E; holding the FY2025 ratio in a year already three-quarters realised understated FY2026E revenue and implied an unexplained Q4 collapse. The gold:copper physical ratio is a mine-plan output, not a price forecast. FY2032E onward steps to 2.18x because Elang's reserve grade is far more gold-rich: 27 Moz Au over 18.17 bn lbs Cu is 3.28 oz of contained gold per tonne of copper [S6, F7], and at an 85% recovery/payable factor that is 2.79 oz sold per tonne of copper, worth 1.09x of copper revenue at the deck's 4,300/11,000 ratio, plus the same ~0.09x other-credit residual. The 85% factor is a standard porphyry-concentrate assumption, not a company disclosure, and it is the largest single estimate in the Elang credit; the FY2025 Batu Hijau outturn (169.55 koz of gold sold on 107.50 kt of copper sold, 1.58 oz/t [F3, F1]) is the sanity check. The step is sourced to the Elang reserve statement, not fitted to a price spike.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No domestic price cap applies to copper or gold; Indonesia's DMO mechanism covers coal, not copper-gold concentrate. The copper export ban/export permit regime affects the timing of concentrate sales, not the price, and the LK shows export permits granted on 31 October 2025 [S2 p.101, S4 p.5].

assumptions.label: Cost intensity factor (1.0 = cost_per_bcm carries cash cost per copper tonne)
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 because this is a metal-content model priced per tonne of copper sold, not a coal-style bcm stripping model; cost_per_bcm therefore carries total cash cost per copper tonne directly. The LK discloses waste and ore tonnages and a unit mining cost, but ore grade and recovery, not bcm, drive payable metal [S2 p.88, S3 p.11].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per copper tonne sold (USD/t, ex-royalty and ex-D&A)
assumptions.basis: Derived exactly as the desk requires: FY2025 COGS of US$1,010.9m less government royalties of US$219.283m [F17] less D&A of US$247.156m [F5] = US$544.46m of cash cost, over 107.50 kt of copper sold [F1] = US$5,064.7/t. This is gross cash cost before by-product credits (the gold and silver credits sit in realisation), and it is held flat in nominal USD through FY2035E because the company gives no cost guidance and the 9M2026 C1 print (US$(0.62)/lb net) is consistent with the same gross cost base once the by-product credit is added back [S3 p.11]. It reconciles to the group's US$1,057m reported EBITDA at the last actual [F18].

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default 0.30 is retained: diesel is a material mining input and the LK notes higher diesel costs in the FY2025 cost movement, but AMMN does not disclose a fuel share of cash cost [S2 p.100]. The brent deck is flat around the forecast, so the term is a small second-order adjustment.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per copper tonne (included in cost_per_bcm)
assumptions.basis: Zero because the entire cash cost is carried in cost_per_bcm at strip_ratio 1.0. Splitting mining from processing is not possible from the LK without a segment cost note, and a fabricated split would not change EBITDA [S2 p.100, S3 p.11].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat)
assumptions.basis: The LK states that in April 2025 the government raised the copper cathode royalty from 2% to 6-7% and gold from 10% to 16%, and FY2025 government royalties were US$219.283m or 11.88% of net sales [S2 p.101, F17]. The engine applies a flat rate to revenue because the model does not split cathode from concentrate, so the rate is the effective one the accounts show: 11.9% (FY2025 11.88%, [F17, S2 p.101]). The 9M2026 cost bridge corroborates it: royalties of US$1.30/lb of copper sold on 131.4 kt is about US$377m, 11.6% of the US$3,238m of 9M2026 net sales [S3 p.6, p.11]. The earlier 13.5% overstated the statutory mix step against both actuals and is replaced; the rate is neither a haircut nor a pad.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero: all of the group's consolidated sales are copper and gold from AMNT, with no separate service or other segment disclosed [S2 p.226].

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Not used: other revenue is zero [S2 p.226].

assumptions.label: D&A per copper tonne sold
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A of US$247.156m [F5] over 107.50 kt of copper sold [F1] = US$2,299/t. FY2024's US$236.876m [F6] over 130.86 kt [F2] is US$1,810/t; the step up is the smelter and refinery entering service, which the LK attributes to higher depreciation from completed projects [S2 p.100]. Held at the FY2025 level as the asset base is now largely built; the Elang build adds depreciation only after 2031 and is left in capex until then.

assumptions.label: Capex per copper tonne sold (sustaining and Elang development)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E US$1,250/t: 9M2026 capex was US$170m, down 84% year on year, and a full year near US$220m over 180 kt is about US$1,250/t [S3 p.6, p.21]. FY2027E US$1,400/t is sustaining plus close-out. FY2028E-FY2031E carry the Elang build at US$6,000-8,000/t of copper sold: the company spent US$1,373m in 2025 on Phase 8, the smelter, the concentrator expansion and the power plant [F15], and Elang is a porphyry of 2.58 bn t requiring a new mine and the second half of the 85 Mtpa plant [S5, S6]; spreading roughly US$6.6bn of development over FY2028E-FY2032E is therefore the company's own recent annual capex intensity, not an unsourced guess. FY2033E onward returns to sustaining US$1,250-1,500/t. The mid-series build is why the FY2026E-to-FY2035E drift is zero while the intervening years spike.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: all capital expenditure is carried per tonne in capex_unit, including the Elang build, so there is no double count [S3, F15].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set to FY2024's 0.337, not the three-year average of 0.53, because FY2025's 0.876 ratio is the 190,000 dmt concentrate stockpile built ahead of the smelter and the refined-metal inventory built during 2026 [S8 p.76, S3 p.21]. With the smelter at design capacity the stockpile unwinds, so the working-capital intensity returns to the pre-commissioning level; the 2026 forecast therefore releases working capital rather than tying up 53% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of US$64.7m on PBT of US$322.7m is 20.0%; the three-year average is 21.3% [S0]. Use 21.0%, inside the statutory 22% corporate rate and the LK's effective charge.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense of US$386.0m on opening debt of US$4,285.5m is 9.0%; the three-year average is 9.55% [S0]. Use 9.5%, consistent with the USD bank facilities and the LK's finance cost [S2 p.102].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: USD cash earns a money-market return; the macro deck's 10-year US Treasury is 4.86% and AMMN holds short-dated USD deposits, so 4.0% is used [S0, S3 p.21]. The pack has no interest-income line, so the yield is supplied rather than defaulted.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero in the base case: management is deleveraging (debt down US$865m in 9M2026 and net debt/EBITDA at 1.9x) and the Elang build is assumed funded from the same operating cash flow and balance-sheet capacity rather than new net debt [S3 p.6, p.21]. Any Elang project financing is upside to the equity value, not modelled.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: FY2025's non-operating items are FX and one-off items already excluded from EBITDA; no recurring other line is disclosed [S2 p.16, p.100].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Three-year average of minority/net profit is 2.29% [S0]; FY2025 minority interest was US$9.1m on net profit of US$258.0m (3.5%). Hold 2.3%, the historical average.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The LK is explicit: "The Company does not anticipate paying any dividends until our major capital expansion programs are completed" [S2 p.107]. The smelter is complete but the Elang programme follows, so the base case assumes no dividend through the forecast; any payout is upside to the equity holder and is not counted in the return.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: the IDR1.0tn buyback announced 22 October 2026 (about US$55m) is small relative to the US$15.8bn market capitalisation and its execution is not disclosed; it is deducted in the valuation bridge as cash leaving the company rather than modelled as a share-count reduction [S3 p.5, F22].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero because the primary method is dcf_life, which stops at the reserve/mine-plan end and has no terminal value; the parameter is not used to extend a depleting asset [S6, F23, F24].

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 opex of US$162.0m on revenue of US$1,846.5m is 8.8%; the three-year average is 7.1% [S0]. Use 7.5%, between the two, because the 2025 ratio includes transition costs and the integrated operation should run at the lower historical level. The choice reproduces FY2025 EBITDA within 1% in the calibration when combined with the royalty line.

challenges.challenge: The scenario override freezes the copper benchmark at the FY2030 value times the shock for all years FY2031-FY2055: bull runs US$12,903 flat and bear US$9,537 flat, against a base that escalates from US$11,673 (FY2032) to US$18,408 (FY2055). Applying the stated -15%/+15% price and -5%/+5% volume shocks to the full escalating path gives bear tp Rp1,970 and bull tp Rp5,153, not the reported Rp1,158/Rp3,940; the weighted target is Rp3,528 (-11.8% TR), not Rp3,021 (-24.5%). The bull therefore exceeds the price, falsifying the summary's "even our bull case is still below the current share price".
challenges.answer: Confirmed and reproduced. Model._apply_overrides writes the shocked copper deck into every forecast label, and deck_value then returns lt*(1+esc)^1 for each later year, so the shocked FY2030 value (11,220) repeats to FY2055. A patched in-memory run that shocks only the explicit years and lt gives bear 1,649 / base 3,499 / bull 5,520 against the engine's 882 / 3,499 / 4,372, a corrected weighted target of about 3,542 rather than 3,063. The one-line fix in cov_engine.Model._apply_overrides is a script edit, which hard law puts outside analyst scope, so the target the engine publishes remains understated; the report now withdraws the bull-below-price and downside-larger claims, states that the engine holds the post-2029 copper path flat against escalating costs, and anchors the rating on the base case, which the defect does not touch. Flagged to OPS for the engine patch.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue US$3,980m, EBITDA US$2,121m and net income US$867m are all below or barely above the 9M2026 actuals of US$3,238m, US$1,833m and US$880m [S3 p.6]. That implies Q4 revenue of US$742m (-37% q/q from Q3's US$1,185m) and Q4 net income of -US$13m against Q3's +US$376m. No operational or price reason for a Q4 collapse is given; §3 instead calls the current year a recovery.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is now reconciled to the 9M2026 actual: revenue 4,436, EBITDA 2,552 and net income 1,228 against 3,238 / 1,833 / 880 reported for nine months, leaving a fourth quarter of about 1,198 of revenue, in line with the third quarter, on 180 kt of copper sold. The gap was the realisation hold, not a Q4 collapse; section 3 now says so explicitly with the 9M figures as facts.

challenges.challenge: Realisation is held at 1.615x, but 9M2026 sales of US$3,238m over 131.4 kt of copper sold is US$24,642/t, or 1.80x the FY2026E deck copper of 13,692. The model's FY2026E ASP of US$22,113 is 11% below the realised run-rate, so the base case understates current-year revenue and cash flow with no sourced reason.
challenges.answer: FY2026E realisation is now 1.80x, the 9M2026 actual (net sales 3,238 over 131.4 kt is 24,642/t, 1.80x the FY2026E deck copper of 13,692), instead of holding the FY2025 1.615x into a year already three-quarters realised; the FY2025 ratio remains the historical anchor only. The resulting positive calibration gap is the 2026 gold credit and is justified with sources in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: The royalty is set at 13.5% flat while FY2025 government royalties were US$219.283m on net sales of US$1,846.5m, an 11.88% effective rate [F17, S2 p.101], and the statutory rates are 6-7% on copper cathode and 16% on gold.
